items.prose: A deployment script receives absolute Unix paths. `.` means here and `..` means up one folder; the root stays the root. Repeated slashes count as one. A name such as `...` is an ordinary name.
items.question: Write `simplify_path(path)`: the shortest equivalent path, with no trailing slash. The root is `/`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests, including `..` at the root, repeated slashes and a folder named `...`.

feedback.correct: Split on `/`, keep a stack of names, pop on `..`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 has a trailing slash. Drop the empty part it leaves.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has `.` and `..`. Skip `.`, and pop on `..`.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is `/../`. `..` at the root does nothing.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has a folder named `...`. Only `.` and `..` are special.

explain.text: Splitting on `/` turns repeated slashes into empty parts, which are skipped. `..` pops a name when there is one. Joining the stack after a single `/` gives the root as `/`.

items.prose: `board` is a rectangle of 0 and 1. A live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours, of its 8, lives on. A dead cell with exactly 3 becomes live. Every other cell is dead next step. Cells beyond the border do not exist.
items.question: Write `life_step(board)`: return the board after one step. Count neighbours on the old board.

tests.setup: b = [[(r * 7 + c * 3) % 5 % 2 for c in range(100)] for r in range(100)]

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests, including a single row and a single live cell. The last sums the live cells of a 100 by 100 board.

feedback.correct: Count on the old board, write a new one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is a blinker: the vertical line becomes horizontal.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is one live cell. It has no neighbours, so it dies.
byKey.test-5: Test 5: if you update cells in place, later cells see new values. Build a new board.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 is a single row. Cells beyond the border do not exist; do not wrap round.

explain.text: Each cell's next value depends only on the old board, so build a new one. Bounds checks stand in for the missing cells beyond the border. The time is $O(8rc)$.

items.prose: `s` holds only `(` and `)`. A valid run is well formed and contiguous: `(()())` is one, `())(` is not. The last test has 100,000 characters.
items.question: Write `longest_valid_parentheses(s)`: the length of the longest valid run.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. The last is 50,000 `(` then 50,000 `)`, so a cubic check runs out of time.

feedback.correct: A stack of indices with a base of −1 measures each valid run as it closes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 is `)(()())(`. A stray `)` resets the base; the run between is 6.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is `()(())`: two valid parts next to each other make one run of 6.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has unmatched `(`s. Only the last `()` is valid: 2.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 has 100,000 characters. Use one pass with a stack, not a check of every substring.

explain.text: The stack holds the index just before the current run, starting with −1. A `)` pops; if the stack empties it becomes the new base, else `i - stack[-1]` is the run's length. Each index is pushed and popped once: $O(n)$.

items.question: Say aloud how you read the bot's statement, on `[300, 297, 299, 298, 295, 291]`.

widget.prompt: Say this aloud, timing yourself to three minutes, then write the main points. Explain how you read the statement of `l8-simulating-the-rules`. Cover the state, the events, the order of checks and the end rule. Then hand-trace the bot on `[300, 297, 299, 298, 295, 291]` and give the result.
widget.model:
**State.** Three values carry from day to day: long or flat, the entry price and the buy day.

**Events.** One event per day: that day's price, with its index $i$.

**Order of checks.** A flat bot on day $i \ge 1$ buys when the price is below the day before. A long bot checks, in this order: take profit ($100p \ge 105 \cdot \text{entry}$), stop ($100p \le 97 \cdot \text{entry}$), then time ($i - \text{bought} = 3$). The first true rule sells. A bot that sells on day $i$ does not buy on day $i$.

**End of data.** A bot still long after the last day sells at the last price, and that counts as a trade.

**Trace.** Day 0 never trades. Day 1: 297 is below 300, so buy at 297. Days 2 and 3 are 299 and 298: $29{,}900$ and $29{,}800$ are below $31{,}185$ and above $28{,}809$. The bot has held 1, then 2 days. Day 4 is 295: no price rule fires ($29{,}500 > 28{,}809$). But $4 - 1 = 3$, so the time rule sells at 295 for $-2$. The bot may not buy on day 4, even though 295 is below 298. Day 5 is 291, below 295, so it buys at 291. The data ends, so it sells at 291 for 0.

**Result.** `[-2, 2]`.

rubric.text: Names the state: long or flat, entry price, buy day
Names the events: one price per day, with day 0 never trading
Gives the order of checks, take profit then stop then time, and the same-day rule
Traces it: buys 297 on day 1, sells 295 on day 4, buys 291 on day 5
States the end-of-data rule and the result `[-2, 2]`

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Mark your answer against the rubric.

explain.text: A good answer names the state, the events and the order of checks. A hand trace on a short list gives a test with a known answer. The end rule is the one most often forgotten.

items.prose: A matrix has 250 rows and 400 columns, filled row by row from 0. Row $r$, column $c$ holds $400r + c$.
items.question: What is the last entry of its clockwise spiral?

feedback.correct: The last lap is a 2 by 152 block, ending at row 125, column 124: 50,124.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find what is left after 124 laps, then where its lap ends.

byKey.rowmajor: 99,999 is last in row order. The spiral ends near the middle.
byKey.swap: You ended on row 124. The last lap comes back along row 125.
byKey.short: You stopped one cell short on the way back along row 125. The lap ends at column 124.

explain.text: Each lap removes two rows and two columns. After 124 laps rows 124 to 125 and columns 124 to 275 remain, a 2 by 152 block. Its lap runs along row 124, down to row 125, then back along row 125 to column 124: $400 \times 125 + 124 = 50{,}124$.

items.question: Put the decoder's rules in the order a single loop over `s` applies them. Leave out the rule that does not belong.

lines.text: On a digit, build the count: `count = count * 10 + int(ch)`
On `[`, push the text so far and the count, then start both afresh
On `]`, pop `(prev, k)`, repeat the current text `k` times and append it to `prev`
On a letter, append it to the current text
After the loop, return the current text joined
On a digit, push it onto the stack as a character
lines.why: A count of 12 would split into 1 and 2. Build the number in `count` instead.

feedback.correct: Four cases inside the loop, in any order, and the return after it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The four cases can come in any order, but the return comes last.

byKey.d1: You pushed the digit as a character. A count of 12 would arrive as two entries.
byKey.left-out: Every rule but one belongs. Only pushing digits is wrong.

explain.text: Each character falls into exactly one case, so the four cases can be checked in any order. The return comes after the loop. Digits build `count`, so `12[x]` repeats 12 times.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run each event against the book in turn.

byKey.cap: You let order 3 buy at 102, above its limit of 101. It takes only order 2's 2 at 101.
byKey.nomarket: You stopped before the market order. It sells 6 into the bids.
byKey.market: You counted only the market sell. Order 3 first traded 2 with order 2.

explain.text: Order 3 buys 2 from order 2 at 101 and rests 2 at 101. The market sell takes those 2 at 101, then 4 of order 4's 5 at 100. That is $2 + 2 + 4 = 8$; 1 rests bid at 100 and 3 offered at 102.

items.question: For prices `[396, 401, 398, 400, 394, 392, 404, 400, 388]`, which result does the bot give with the time rule written correctly, `i - bought == 3`?

options.why: That is the rule written `> 3`: it sells a day late, at 404 instead of 392.
That is the rule written `== 2`: it sells a day early, at 394.
That is the bot with no time rule: it holds from 398 to the end and sells at 388.

feedback.correct: Buy 398 on day 2 and sell 392 on day 5. Buy 400 on day 7 and stop out at 388 on day 8.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace with `i - bought == 3` and the rules in order.

explain.text: Day 2 buys 398 and day 5, three days on, sells at 392 for $-6$. Day 7 buys 400, and day 8's 388 hits the stop, $38{,}800 \le 38{,}800$, for $-12$. Total `[-18, 2]`.
